vulnerability: Arbitrary external call allows unauthorized minting via MinterProxy privileges
reason: The swap function is externally callable and allows the caller to control both target and callData. In the non-native branch, the initial safeTransferFrom is performed on tokenAddr, which can be an attacker-controlled fake ERC20 that simply returns true without transferring any real value. The contract then executes target.functionCall(callData) from the MinterProxy address. Because MinterProxy is intended to hold minter/controller privileges on token contracts, an attacker can set target to a real token where MinterProxy is authorized to mint and set callData to mint(attacker, hugeAmount). The subsequent balance check uses receiveToken, which can be another attacker-controlled fake token whose balanceOf returns an increased value. The attacker therefore mints arbitrary tokens without owning any real assets. This is exploitable by any external account and is critical.

vulnerability: Unlimited token approval to arbitrary target enables draining of all token balances
reason: In the non-native branch, after pulling amount of tokenAddr from the caller, the function calls safeApprove(target, MAX_UINT256) for the caller-supplied target whenever the current allowance is below amount. This gives an arbitrary attacker-controlled contract an unlimited allowance over tokenAddr held by MinterProxy. The target can immediately call tokenAddr.transferFrom(MinterProxy, attacker, tokenAddr.balanceOf(MinterProxy)) to steal the entire token balance, including user funds held when the contract acts as its own liquidpool and any pending fees. The approval is never reset. The new_balance > old_balance check can be satisfied with a fake receiveToken, so the theft succeeds. Even if the attacker only deposits 1 wei of tokenAddr, they can drain the full balance of that token from the contract.

vulnerability: Spoofable balance check via attacker-controlled receiveToken
reason: The swap function measures the output amount by calling IERC20(receiveToken).balanceOf(address(this)) before and after the arbitrary target call. The receiveToken address is entirely caller-controlled and is not checked against the actual token returned by the target. A malicious receiveToken contract can return different values on successive balanceOf calls (e.g., 0 for the first call and 1 for the second), making new_balance > old_balance and _amountOut >= minAmount pass even though the target call produced no real tokens for MinterProxy. This allows an attacker to bypass the swap output validation and execute arbitrary privileged calls through target while only transferring worthless fake tokens to the receiver. Combined with the arbitrary call, this enables minting or draining of real assets via MinterProxy.
